extracted.intended_audience: university technology transfer offices, university counsel, research administrators, and university researchers involved in patenting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for university technology transfer and research offices on patent-related risks and defenses (experimental use, sovereign immunity, Hatch-Waxman, §1498), publication/on-sale/public-use bars, and inventorship/assignment issues affecting university research and patenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use defense (two branches)
rubrics_metrics.description: The experimental use defense has two branches: the ascertain validity branch (practicing a patented invention to check/test validity) and the philosophical experiment branch (use 'solely for amusement, to satisfy idle curiosity, or for strictly philosophical inquiry').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The defense is extremely narrow. After Madey v. Duke University, the philosophical experiment branch does not immunize conduct that is 'in keeping with the alleged infringer’s legitimate business,' including university activities that further legitimate institutional objectives (educating/enlightening students and faculty). Universities may still assert it for one-time academic experiments, but should not rely on it for ongoing research; better, more reliable defenses should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: State sovereign immunity under the Eleventh Amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: State universities may be immune from patent infringement suits under the Eleventh Amendment, shielding research (commercial or noncommercial) conducted at state institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Florida Prepaid held Congress did not properly abrogate states’ sovereign immunity for patent suits. Immunity can be waived by voluntary participation in litigation; waiver must be truly voluntary (Xechem). Universities must guard against inadvertent waiver (e.g., suit over ownership between university and faculty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hatch-Waxman Act safe harbor (FDA-related testing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Drug Price Competition and Patent Term Restoration Act provides immunity from suit where testing of a patented invention is for the purpose of securing FDA regulatory approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to drugs and medical devices (Eli Lilly v. Medtronic) and, per Merck v. Integra, can cover preclinical research if 'reasonably related' to a potential FDA submission. Protection may apply even if results are not ultimately submitted to FDA or are for new drugs/new uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal contractor defense under 28 U.S.C. §1498(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: 28 U.S.C. §1498(a) makes the United States’ remedy for patent infringement 'reasonable compensation' and provides immunity for federal contractors when infringement is 'by or for' the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope for university researchers is unclear post-Madey; applicability depends on grant/contract terms and whether the activity is 'by or for the United States' with 'authorization and consent' of the government. Madey suggested close scrutiny of grant terms; further case development may clarify requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute novelty / publication bars (international vs. U.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most countries outside the U.S. adopt an absolute novelty standard: any public disclosure of the invention to persons not under confidentiality before filing destroys patent rights. The U.S. provides a one-year grace period from publication, public use, or on-sale event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universities must anticipate publications, presentations, and studies; file patent applications before public dissemination when possible to preserve foreign patent rights. Some countries (e.g., Canada exceptions) may still provide limited grace but treat pre-filing disclosure as fatal in many jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Klopfenstein factors for when a scientific presentation is a 'publication'
rubrics_metrics.description: A presentation at a scientific meeting may be a publication if it is 'publicly accessible.' The Federal Circuit articulated three factors: (1) whether the presentation was shown for an extended period to members of the public having the relevant level of knowledge (persons of ordinary skill in the art); (2) whether those members were precluded from taking notes or photographs; and (3) whether the presentation was given in such a way that copying the information would be relatively simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An entirely oral presentation with neither slides nor copies is not a publication per Klopfenstein, but may still be a public use. Universities should review and clear presentations (oral or printed) to scientific meetings to manage bar risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral presentations may create a public-use bar even if not a publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if an oral presentation without slides/copies is not a publication, it may still be considered a public use of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universities should clear such presentations because public use (not just publication) can start statutory bars; apply confidentiality or delay public disclosures until filing where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use statutory bar criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Two primary factors determine public use: (1) whether the use was public (not kept secret or under confidentiality), and (2) whether the invention existed in a sufficiently definable form at the time of use (e.g., prototype or description enabling practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An invention is 'ready for patenting' when reduced to practice or when drawings/descriptions are specific enough to enable a person skilled in the art (Pfaff v. Wells). Experimental testing arguments can be scrutinized; courts evaluate whether the testing was necessary to define the claimed invention or merely to establish efficacy/safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical studies can trigger public-use or on-sale bars (exercise caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clinical testing may be treated as non-experimental and thus as public use or on-sale activity if it is not needed to define the claimed invention (e.g., measuring efficacy rather than defining the drug).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SmithKline Beecham initially held clinical trials can be invalidating public use; the Federal Circuit later vacated that initial ruling en banc, but the area remains risky. Universities should file patents early when planning clinical studies or external dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-sale statutory bar vs. offers to license
rubrics_metrics.description: An on-sale statutory bar arises from offers for sale of a tangible item (device, product, drug). By contrast, offers to sell/transfer/license the intangible patent rights do not create an on-sale statutory bar; royalties do not convert a license into a sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensing negotiations and offers to license production/marketing rights generally do not create on-sale bars (In re Kollar; Elan v. Andrx). Inclusion of pricing for future supply does not necessarily create an on-sale bar if critical commercial terms (formulation, ingredient costs, packaging) are not determinable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing of process/method technologies has low on-sale bar risk
rubrics_metrics.description: For process or method technologies, selling know-how or details is unlikely to create an on-sale statutory bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universities that license process/method technologies are at low risk of triggering on-sale bars because tangible sale of embodiments is typically required for the bar to run.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship is a question of law (conception + reduction to practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventorship requires legal determination of who contributed to the claimed invention based on conception and reduction to practice (conception is primary; reduction to practice can also contribute).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventorship is distinct from authorship. Incorrect inventorship can invalidate a patent (and cannot be corrected if the error involved deceptive intent). The determination should be made by the registered patent attorney/agent drafting the application to provide an objective, legally sound analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception standard for inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception occurs 'when the idea is so clearly defined in the inventor’s mind that only ordinary skill would be necessary to reduce the invention to practice, without extensive research or experimentation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conception is joint, it is sufficient that without a person's contribution the final conception would have been 'less' in some beneficial sense (less efficient, simple, economical, etc.). Interviews and documentation of contributions are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint inventorship criteria and borderline non-inventive contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Joint inventorship requires collaborative contributions to the conception. Non-inventive activities include following directions in reduction to practice, making obvious improvements, merely suggesting a result, contributing only an insufficient portion of the invention, providing publicly available information, or contributing ideas that are part of the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even geographically separated contributors can be joint inventors if their communications led to joint conception. Case examples (University of Colorado Foundation; Oregon Health & Science University) illustrate when contributions do or do not suffice for inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of contribution affects inventorship (post-filing discoveries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributions that occur after the patent is filed (later discoveries) typically do not create inventorship on an earlier-filed patent covering earlier subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an inventive contribution arises after initial conception and after filing, the contributor may not be a joint inventor for that earlier application (Vertex example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correcting omitted inventors after grant (stringent standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: An omitted inventor can be added after grant only with proof that the omission occurred without deceptive intent and with clear and convincing evidence of the omitted inventor's contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the standard is stringent and can work against the university, the practical rule is: 'when in doubt, and if there is a supportable basis, add the researcher' as an inventor at filing to avoid later problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtaining assignments/transfer of title from inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities should obtain a transfer (assignment) of title from inventors to secure clear title to patents. An assignment is not required to file, but without it licensing/enforcement efforts can be jeopardized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt execution of assignments from inventors is preferable. In the absence of an assignment, licensees or others may assert defects (e.g., Trustees of Boston University v. Beacon Laboratories) and challenge university rights. Secure assignments near the time of filing to avoid title disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the patent attorney in inventorship and filing process
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent attorney drafting the application should determine inventorship and advise regarding assignment and correction procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The attorney has the legal training to determine inventorship, provide an objective determination that can be corrected if needed, and should be responsible for resolving inventorship questions rather than leaving it solely to university managers or researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative systems to manage publications, presentations, and patent filing timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities must put systems in place to anticipate publications, presentations, and studies to avoid inadvertent loss of patent rights through public disclosure, public use, or on-sale events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement disclosure review, clearance procedures for conference presentations (including oral presentations), and timely patent filings prior to public dissemination. Special attention is required for clinical studies and collaborations with industry to preserve patentability.
